source.title: Single dose creatine improves cognitive performance and induces changes in cerebral high energy phosphates during sleep deprivation

paper.citation: Gordji-Nejad A., Matusch A., Kleedörfer S., Jayeshkumar Patel H., Drzezga A., Elmenhorst D., et al. Single dose creatine improves cognitive performance and induces changes in cerebral high energy phosphates during sleep deprivation. Scientific Reports. 2024;14(1):4937. doi:10.1038/s41598-024-54249-9.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does one high dose of creatine monohydrate alter cerebral energy metabolites, subjective fatigue, and cognitive performance during overnight sleep deprivation? Fifteen healthy adults, including eight women, aged 20–28 completed two supervised overnight laboratory sessions. Participants had no reported sleep, neurologic, psychiatric, substance-use, smoking, or medication issues and standardized sleep timing before sessions. This was a double-blind, randomized, balanced crossover trial. Each participant received creatine monohydrate at 0.35 g/kg on one night and corn-starch placebo on another, separated by at least five days.
paper.tldr: Compared with placebo, creatine reduced the pooled subjective fatigue score at 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. by 8%. Pooled across three postdose time points, word-memory accuracy improved by 10.3%, and processing time improved for word memory, language, logic, and numeric tasks. The study supports further research on creatine as an acute countermeasure to sleep-loss-related cognitive decline.
paper.methods: This was a double-blind, randomized, balanced crossover trial. Each participant received creatine monohydrate at 0.35 g/kg on one night and corn-starch placebo on another, separated by at least five days. During approximately 21 hours of wakefulness, cognition, fatigue, and cerebral metabolites were repeatedly assessed using a test battery, 31P-MRS, and 1H-MRS.
paper.findings: Compared with placebo, creatine reduced the pooled subjective fatigue score at 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. by 8%. Pooled across three postdose time points, word-memory accuracy improved by 10.3%, and processing time improved for word memory, language, logic, and numeric tasks. Creatine altered cerebral phosphate measures, including regional increases in PCr/31P and reductions in Pi/31P, and prevented the sleep-deprivation-associated fall in pH in measured regions. Cognitive and metabolic effects were observed from about 3.5 hours after ingestion and persisted through the final measurement ending about nine hours after dosing. Correlations between regional metabolite changes and cognitive changes were exploratory associations and do not prove that the measured metabolite shifts mediated performance.
paper.limitations: The sample was only 15 healthy young adults in a tightly controlled laboratory crossover, not athletes performing physical work, travel, or competition. The dose of 0.35 g/kg is substantially higher than common single maintenance doses, and the article does not establish an optimal or routine dose. Many cognitive tasks, time points, voxels, and metabolites were analyzed; although Bonferroni thresholds were used for parts of the analysis, multiplicity and regional-selection complexity remain important. Voxel coverage was limited, circadian effects could have contributed to ATP changes, and proposed uptake mechanisms are inferential. Safety and effectiveness with repeated use, dehydration, heat, renal risk, or other supplements were not established.
paper.practicalImplications: The study supports further research on creatine as an acute countermeasure to sleep-loss-related cognitive decline. It does not justify using 0.35 g/kg as a team protocol or as a substitute for sleep. Any applied consideration should go through sports medicine and sports nutrition, with attention to medical history, product quality, gastrointestinal tolerance, hydration context, and governing-body policy. For operations, prioritize sleep opportunity, travel planning, and fatigue-aware decision design; treat supplementation as a secondary, clinically governed option.
